title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
description: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by relinking the existing nodes.
statement:
Write `merge_two_lists(first, second)`, which merges two sorted linked lists into one sorted list and returns its head. `ListNode` is given: each node has a `val` and a `next`. Both lists are sorted in ascending order and may contain equal values.

- Reuse the existing nodes: relink their `next` pointers instead of creating new nodes.
- When two values are equal, the node from `first` comes before the node from `second`.
- Either list may be empty (`None`). If both are, return `None`.

**Examples**

```
1 -> 2 -> 4   and   1 -> 3 -> 4    merge into    1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 4
None          and   1 -> 3 -> 4    merge into    1 -> 3 -> 4
None          and   None           merge into    None
```
hints: At every step only the two front nodes matter. Which of them has to come next in the merged list?
Keep a `tail` pointer at the end of the merged list. Attach the smaller front node to `tail.next`, advance that list and `tail`, and repeat. When one list is empty, attach the rest of the other.
A dummy node placed before the head means the first node needs no special case: build after it and return `dummy.next`. Use `<=` so that a tie takes the node from `first`.
explanation:
**The idea.** The smallest remaining value is always at the front of one of the two lists. So keep a `tail` at the end of the merged list so far, repeatedly take the smaller front node, hang it on `tail`, and move that list forward. When one list runs out, the other is already sorted, so attach all of it in one move.

**The dummy node.** The merged list's head is not known until the first comparison. Starting from a dummy node in front of everything means the first node is attached like any other, and `dummy.next` is the answer.

**Equal values.** Comparing with `<=` takes from `first` on a tie, so equal values keep their original order. That is what makes a merge *stable*, and it is the merge step of merge sort on a linked list.

**Complexity.** O(n + m) time. O(1) extra space, because the nodes are relinked, not copied. A recursive version (merge the heads, then merge the rest) is shorter but uses one stack frame per node, which fails on long lists in Python.

**Follow-up.** Merge `k` sorted lists: repeatedly take the smallest front node of all `k` lists with a heap, in O(N log k).
